additional_practice.prompt: A disease rate rises from 20% to 30%. What is the increase in percentage points? Choose one: A 10; B 20; C 30; D 50.

Each potato piece starts at 2.00 g. Calculate its percentage change in mass using the final masses below. Plot percentage change against concentration and estimate the concentration giving no net mass change.

| Concentration (mol/dm³) | Final mass (g) |
|---|---|
| 0.00 | 2.20 |
| 0.10 | 2.10 |
| 0.20 | 2.00 |
| 0.30 | 1.90 |
| 0.40 | 1.80 |
additional_practice.answer:
Use **(final − initial)/initial × 100**. The percentage changes are **+10%, +5%, 0%, −5% and −10%** respectively.

Plot concentration on the **horizontal axis** and percentage mass change on the **vertical axis**, with units and suitable regular scales. Plot the five points and draw the best-fit straight line. It crosses 0% at **0.20 mol/dm³**, the estimate of no net mass change.

![The percentage-mass-change line crosses zero at a concentration of 0.20 mol/dm³.](../Diagrams/osmosis-percentage-model.svg)

additional_practice.prompt: A pupil moves a lamp from 20 cm to 10 cm from pondweed. Bubble counts in two minutes rise from 36 to 60, while water temperature rises from 20°C to 26°C. There are no repeat trials. The pupil concludes: “Halving distance doubles light intensity, and this proves the higher light intensity increases the photosynthesis rate by 67% in all plants.” Evaluate this conclusion using calculations and the method.
additional_practice.answer:
- Under the inverse-square model, intensity changes by (20/10)² = **4**, so it **quadruples**, rather than doubles.
- Bubble rates are 36 ÷ 2 = **18 bubbles/min** and 60 ÷ 2 = **30 bubbles/min**.
- Percentage increase = (30 − 18) ÷ 18 × 100 = **66.7%**, so the numerical claim is reasonable for the **observed bubble-rate change**.
- However, temperature also changed and affects enzyme activity. This comparison does not isolate light intensity. Use a water bath or suitable heat shield and monitor temperature.
- Bubble size can vary. Measuring oxygen volume per unit time is a better measure of gas production.
- Repeat each setting, compare means and use several suitable plants before generalising. One unreplicated, confounded comparison cannot establish the same effect in all plants.
